paragraphs: I did clerkships for two months at the University of Western Australia (UWA).

In the first month I did my clerkship in neurosurgery at Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital (SCGH) in Perth. Perth is a major city of WA state, and SCGH, with about 600 beds, receives patients referred from the entire state. Neurosurgery had 21 specialists and was full of energy.

The weekday schedule was: 7 a.m. rounds, observing about three operations, and finishing around 18:00 (longest 6:00 to 23:00). In addition there were daily outpatient clinics, a weekly conference and lectures for residents, a Saturday morning study session for specialists, and emergency operations at night and on holidays. What to take part in was entirely up to me. Wanting to protect my daily rhythm, I did not go to emergency operations.

I observed 51 operations, 60% of them brain and 40% spine. I entered the surgical field in 31 of them, and although at a student level, my technique gradually got a little better. Checking the wounds of patients whose incisions I had closed on rounds from the next day onward was nerve-racking. On days when surgery ended early or when I thought observation was unproductive, I observed outpatient clinics or read charts and manuals for trainees on the ward, so I had no trouble spending my time. What I regret is that I could not take part in ward management. However, considering that visiting students' electronic chart accounts cannot see lab data, that deciphering the paper charts is hard, and that the local students do not touch it either, I also think that learning ward management is unrealistic.

The doctors who left their home countries to throw themselves into competition, full of ambition and undaunted by their busyness, have become my role models. Devoting your life to work is not something to be mocked, and I thought that without that resolve one cannot become a neurosurgeon.

The doctors had no time to teach students step by step, and answering the occasional difficult question quickly and making an impression was hard. At the same time, the UWA students rotating with me were very kind, and my timing was fortunate. Thanks to them the clerkship was fulfilling.

In the second month I did my clerkship at Karratha Health Campus (KHC) in Karratha, a seaside town surrounded by wilderness and mines. When you request rural medicine on the exchange program, you are assigned to one of the country towns scattered across the vast WA state. KHC is a very clean hospital that had been open only six months. You can choose by the week among the emergency department, obstetrics, ward, allied medicine and psychiatry, but since I had come all this way I wanted to choose the busiest department, so I chose the emergency department for all four weeks.

A characteristic was that there were many Indigenous people, whom I had hardly seen in Perth, as well as sailors on temporary port calls and mine workers, and the patients' age group was younger than in Japanese emergency departments. Before arriving I had worried that a rural area might have few patients, but patients are referred from the surrounding area, so there was no need to worry.

From 7:30 to 18:00 my work was to take histories and examine patients with mild to moderate conditions, present to the senior doctor, and then help with ordering tests, procedures, prescriptions and charting. I was entrusted with all the basic procedures, and sometimes even did procedures under anesthesia in the operating room. It was such a flawless environment for getting a head start on initial residency that I gave up half of my days off too to study. Through many failures I gradually became able to do more, and feeling with my own eyes and hands the diseases I had known only from textbooks is beyond compare.

KHC is a regional base hospital, but its facilities are not complete and the doctors' specialties are limited. The style of consulting difficult cases with hospitals in the neighboring town and in Perth and transferring them as necessary was truly the essence of Australian remote-area medicine.
I was given the very valuable experience of taking part in both the highest-level medicine in Australia and the medicine that supports remote areas, and I deeply thank everyone concerned.
